subject: Turning customer needs into a practical design
hook: Count it before we draw it.
ig:
Count it before we draw it.

It sounds dull, but a rough inventory is the most useful thing you can bring to a design consultation.

"More storage" isn't a brief. "Fourteen shirts, six long dresses, two winter coats and about twenty pairs of shoes" is.

Why counting changes the design:

Long items need full-height hanging. Short ones can double up with two rails.
Folded items suit drawers or shelves at a sensible height.
Shoes and boots need depth, and boots need height too.
In a kitchen, the number of pans and tins decides drawer depths.
In a living room, the number of books, games and consoles decides shelf spacing.

It doesn't need to be exact. Ten minutes with your phone notes will do.

What would be the hardest thing to count in your house? Tell us in the comments, and see our made-to-measure furniture via the link in bio.
fb:
Here's a little job that makes a big difference to fitted furniture: count your stuff.

Not to the last sock. Just roughly how many shirts, long coats, pairs of shoes, pans or books you need to store. It tells us whether you need double hanging or full-height, drawers or shelves, and how deep everything should be.

It's the difference between "more storage" and storage that fits your things.

What would be the hardest thing to count in your house? Go on, tell us.
